text:
The quality of leads from Bark.com is so poor yet the prices are so high.

They operate credit system where leads cost X amount of credits and you have to but in bulk. Each credit costs £1.72 once VAT is taken in to account.

Each lead costs on average 40 tokens so a lead is around £70 on average. 

For that lead cost you would expect at least a decent connection rate, but on average 1 in 5 leads respond, and that's after contacting within 60 seconds of a lead registering on the system.

My issue has been raised with them multiple times whilst testing the platform and they are automated responses or no improvement.

If you want to offer services and make money as a business do not use Bark.com. Lead cost and quality do not match.

Basically it feels a bit sketchy and I'd avoid if you're keen on keeping your info close.

I have used Bark for my business and unfortunately I no longer consider it good value for money.

The fundamental problem is that tradespeople pay credits simply to contact potential customers. In my experience, a significant number of those customers then don’t answer the phone, don’t reply to messages, or appear to be using the platform simply to obtain multiple prices with no real commitment to proceed or even engage. 

This means businesses can spend a considerable amount purchasing credits without ever having a genuine opportunity to quote for the work. I have requested credits back on a number of occasions where leads have gone nowhere, been duplicated by those searching for a better price and these requests are often declined.

A recent experience summed up the problem particularly well. A customer repeatedly advertised essentially the same small job over a period of days at different budgets while multiple tradespeople competed for it. Every tradesperson paying to make contact is potentially spending money, regardless of whether the customer ultimately engages them.

I accept that no lead-generation service can guarantee that a customer will choose you. That’s part of business. My issue is paying to access people who don’t meaningfully engage at all, combined with a credit-refund system that in my experience offers insufficient protection when that happens.

For small local businesses, the cost of unsuccessful Bark leads can quickly outweigh the value of the work actually obtained.i

I would spend the same money marketing directly to local customers and generating my own enquiries.  If you’re new to business get leaflets and get your steps up, get your family involved and watch out for nippy wee dogs. 

One star based on my experience and the value received

I rarely leave negative reviews, but Bark’s customer service genuinely shocked me.

I spent over £100 on credits and didn’t get a single job from them. They refunded the credits back to my Bark account, which is apparently their policy, but completely refused to refund the money back to my original payment method.

Normally I’d accept that, but I explained my circumstances. I’d recently lost my job, was going through a formal grievance, and was facing serious financial hardship. I wasn’t asking for anything unreasonable - I simply asked them to make an exception so I could access money I’d already paid while I got back on my feet. I even told them I fully intended to come back and use Bark again once my situation had improved.

Instead, I got the same copy-and-paste policy response over and over again. No empathy. No understanding. No willingness to exercise any discretion whatsoever.

Policies exist for a reason, but good customer service is about recognising when exceptional circumstances deserve an exceptional response. Bark had every opportunity to show a bit of humanity and chose not to.

If you’re happy dealing with a company that sticks rigidly to policy regardless of the situation their customers are in, then Bark may be fine for you. Personally, I’ll remember how I was treated when I needed understanding the most.

text:
I have reached the point where I have decided to cancel my Bark subscription because, for my industry, it simply does not provide value for money.

I run a home companionship and domiciliary care business, and leads in this category are extremely expensive. On average, it costs around 24 credits just to contact one customer. At approximately £1.88 per credit, buying £164 worth of credits only allows me to contact around four or five people.

The problem is that many of those leads never respond. When someone eventually does reply, it is often to say they are no longer looking for the service. Most of these conversations happen over the phone, so when I submit a credit review request, Bark asks me to provide evidence. They often tell me they were unable to verify the customer's response themselves and therefore require me to prove that the lead was no longer valid.

This is what I find most frustrating. If Bark cannot verify the validity of the leads on its own platform, how is a service provider expected to do so? I have found myself sending follow-up text messages to customers, asking them to confirm in writing that they are no longer looking for the service purely so I can request a refund for the credits I paid. Some customers reply, but most do not. It is unreasonable to expect providers to chase customers for evidence just to recover credits.

Over time, I estimate I have spent around £1,400 on Bark, in addition to paying the monthly subscription fee. Although I have secured two clients through the platform, the overall return has not justified the amount I have invested. The cost of the leads, combined with the difficulty of recovering credits for invalid leads, makes the platform far too expensive for my business.

I believe Bark should take greater responsibility for verifying leads before charging professionals and should operate a much fairer and more transparent credit refund process. Businesses should not have to prove something that the platform itself says it cannot verify.

Unfortunately, this will be the last month I purchase Bark credits. I cannot continue investing this amount of money for such poor value and an unfair refund process.

text:
Bark has the potential to be a useful platform, and the website itself is easy to use. However, after purchasing multiple credit packages and Bark Premium, I haven't secured a single client.

The biggest issue isn't the number of enquiries—it's the quality and filtering. A significant proportion of leads either never respond after you've spent credits, or they're private individuals, students or very small businesses with extremely limited budgets. Many of the projects I saw were in the £250–£950 range, with some considerably lower.

For that reason, I think Bark currently works best for low to mid-skilled freelancers who are happy to take on smaller projects. If you're an established agency or a senior consultant whose projects typically start at several thousand pounds, the platform is much harder to justify commercially.

There are two improvements that I believe would make a huge difference:

• Require business enquiries to include a registered company name (verified where possible via Companies House filter) so providers can distinguish genuine businesses from speculative enquiries.

• Allow providers to filter leads by annual turnover, rather than just service category and location or size (a SME that does £100k revenue and one that does £700k will have much more regular and better budgeted work). Not every provider is targeting the same type of client, and the platform should reflect that.

I genuinely hope Bark continues to improve because the concept is strong. Better qualification and filtering would make it a much more valuable platform for established agencies and experienced professionals, not just freelancers competing for lower-value work.

Instead, I spent a considerable amount of money on credits without any return on my investment. Many leads either never replied, had already hired someone, or simply disappeared after I paid to contact them. As a small business owner, paying for leads that never convert is incredibly frustrating and financially damaging.

I understand that no platform can guarantee work, but I expected the leads to be of a much higher quality considering the amount of money required to contact them.

Based on my personal experience, I cannot recommend Bark. I lost money, invested a lot of time following up with potential clients, and received absolutely no jobs in return. I hope Bark reviews its lead verification process and pricing so that professionals receive better value for the money they spend.

text:
Après 3 ans en tant que cliente de Bark, je suis aujourd'hui très déçue de l'évolution de la plateforme.

L'un des principaux problèmes concerne la qualité des prospects. 
En tant que thérapeute, je constate qu'une grande partie des personnes qui arrivent via Bark recherchent en réalité des services gratuits ou remboursés. 
Lorsque l'on tape "psy remboursé" sur Google dans le cadre du dispositif Mon Parcours Psy, l'une des premières réponses affichées est une publicité Bark. Certes, cela permet à Bark de générer du trafic, mais sur le terrain, cela se traduit par des prospects qui ne correspondent pas du tout à nos services payants.
Résultat : perte d'argent, perte de temps et perte d'énergie pour les professionnels qui achètent des crédits en toute bonne foi.

Autre point très frustrant : le manque de transparence concernant les prospects. 
De nombreux professionnels ne signalent pas lorsqu'un prospect a déjà trouvé un prestataire ou lorsqu'il indique rechercher un autre type de service. Nous continuons donc à dépenser des crédits pour contacter des personnes qui ne sont plus intéressées ou qui ne correspondent pas à notre activité.

Enfin, je trouve la communication sur les crédits trompeuse. Lorsque l'on achète 35 crédits, il est indiqué que cela représente environ 5 prospects, ce qui laisse penser à un coût moyen de 7 crédits par prospect. 
Dans la réalité, la plupart des prospects coûtent entre 10 et 14 crédits. Avec 35 crédits, on obtient donc souvent seulement 3 contacts potentiels, et encore sans aucune garantie de retour.

Je comprends que le principe de Bark repose sur la mise en relation, mais la qualité des prospects et le rapport coût/résultat se sont fortement dégradés au fil des années. Aujourd'hui, je ne considère plus cet investissement comme rentable pour mon activité.

text:
Bark is a tricky platform, and this is coming from someone who has been using it for several years as a service provider.

If you're thinking of making a living from Bark, there is a real chance you'll be disappointed. I've spent a lot of money on the platform. I've made money too, so I'm not saying it never works, but the biggest winner in the Bark ecosystem is Bark itself.

Bark spends heavily on Google advertising and attracts lots of potential customers. The problem is that many of those customers have no idea that tradespeople and service providers have to pay to contact them (not saying its not in the fine print but who reads that as a customer). They post an enquiry, browse around, then disappear.

As a trader, you can easily spend £20 to £40, sometimes more, to contact a single lead. In my experience, a large percentage never reply to messages, never answer calls, and never engage at all. Whether they were genuinely interested, changed their mind, made a mistake, or were simply browsing, the result is the same: you've paid, they've vanished, and Bark keeps the money.

When you raise concerns, Bark will usually point you towards their terms and conditions. They may sympathise, but sympathy doesn't refund credits. Meanwhile, if five traders each pay £40 to contact the same lead, Bark could have made £200 or more from that one enquiry regardless of whether any work is ever awarded. There is a 10 percent chance of getting credits back and I their common line is this 

"Thank you for getting in touch and for taking the time to explain the situation.
 
We're sorry to hear you've had issues with this lead. 
 
Unfortunately, we couldn't verify the issue with your lead, so we're unable to refund the credits used."

I've even had customers tell me they posted an advert by mistake and contacted Bark to explain. Some have sent me screenshots showing this. I've then requested a refund, only to be told Bark couldn't verify the situation. In some cases, Bark said they couldn't reach the customer, while the customer told me nobody had contacted them. At that point, you're left wondering who to believe and who has the financial incentive to keep the credits.

Does Bark work? Sometimes, yes. I've won jobs and made money through it. For someone starting out, it can be a source of leads. But go in with your eyes open.

Treat Bark like a roulette wheel, not a guaranteed marketing strategy. Budget for losses. Expect many leads to go nowhere. Understand that you'll often be paying for the opportunity to compete, not for genuine customer engagement.

Can you make money? Yes. I have a 17 percent success rate.

Will you lose money? Almost certainly.

And at the end of the day, the house usually wins.

I’ve been using Bark for quite some time, and while the platform works well in terms of connecting service providers with potential clients, my overall experience has been very frustrating.
The biggest issue is how credits are handled. On multiple occasions, credits were deducted without any meaningful action from my side. For example, I once tried to simply check pricing or credit options, and the system directly charged my credit card without a clear confirmation step. That was already concerning.
More recently, the situation has become worse. When leads come via email, even opening the email or clicking to view basic details (not even contacting the client) results in immediate credit deduction. This has happened multiple times over the past few months, including very recently again. This feels unfair—users should only be charged when they intentionally choose to contact a lead.
Another major concern is customer support. I raised complaints about these issues more than once, but the tickets were closed quickly without proper investigation or resolution. That creates a lack of trust in the platform.
Additionally, the quality of leads is inconsistent. A noticeable number of leads appear questionable—contact numbers don’t work or clients are unresponsive—yet they are marked as “verified.” This raises serious concerns about lead authenticity.
From a business perspective, it’s very difficult to justify the return on investment. With frequent credit deductions and inconsistent lead quality, it becomes hard to recover the money spent, let alone make a profit.
In summary:
Platform concept is good
Credit system feels unfair and unclear
Customer support is unresponsive
Lead quality is inconsistent
I would strongly recommend proceeding with caution and closely monitoring your credit usage if you decide to use this platform.

text:
I have had a very disappointing experience with Bark.com as a tradesman.

One of the biggest issues is that clients are often not aware that tradespeople must purchase credits just to respond to their leads. From a tradesman’s perspective, this creates a very unbalanced system. You pay upfront simply to send a message, with no guarantee of any reply. Realistically, out of 10 leads, you are lucky if 2 even respond.

Another major problem is that many clients leave their job requests active even after they have already hired someone. Tradesmen continue spending money just to receive a short reply like, “I already hired someone.” In some cases, you can spend €20 or more just to find that out. That is extremely frustrating and financially draining.

It is also common that when a client creates a job, the request is automatically sent to five or more tradespeople. This is simply too many. By the time some professionals respond, the job is often already taken. There should be a limit of 2–3 tradespeople per request to avoid unnecessary spending and prevent professionals from paying for leads that are no longer available.

The platform also seems to attract many unqualified individuals offering services at unrealistically low prices. These operators undercut the market and drive prices down to unsustainable levels for legitimate, skilled tradesmen. As professionals, we invest in proper tools, insurance, experience, and high-quality materials - and that naturally reflects in our pricing.

Unfortunately, many clients compare quotes purely on price rather than quality or professionalism. They often choose the cheapest option but still expect a flawless, high-end result. This creates unrealistic expectations and further damages industry standards.

Finally, the credit refund process is practically impossible. Even in clearly unfair situations, there is no realistic way to recover lost credits. If a client has a “verified” phone number, you are automatically excluded from any refund request. It does not matter if they never reply to messages, do not answer phone calls, or ignore emails - the system still treats the lead as valid simply because the phone number is verified. In reality, that verification means nothing if the client is completely unresponsive.

Overall, the system feels heavily weighted against tradespeople, with high costs, very low return, and very little protection for serious professionals trying to run a proper business. The platform should focus more on supporting real, qualified tradesmen with genuine reputations rather than prioritising credit sales. There should be better lead control, fairer refund policies, and stronger quality standards to create a balanced and professional marketplace.

Until that balance changes, it is difficult to see this platform as a sustainable solution for serious tradespeople.

I am a professional builder and my experience with Bark has been extremely disappointing and costly.

Bark uses misleading practices to push professionals into spending credits without receiving real value. Credits are deducted simply by clicking “View details” or accidentally pressing “Contact”, especially on mobile where the buttons are placed extremely close together. One accidental click = money gone, with no confirmation step.

What is even more concerning is the use of very large “tender-style” opportunities, such as £10m–£60m+ Design & Build projects allegedly linked to public bodies (e.g. Crown Estate). These listings are clearly designed to look serious and high-value, but they have no place on a platform like Bark and are completely unrealistic for how real public procurement works.

These “big tenders” strongly encourage professionals to click out of curiosity or hope, only to immediately lose credits. In reality, such projects are procured through official frameworks and tender portals — not Bark. This feels deliberately misleading.

I have spent over £700 in credits without securing a single job. Many leads either never respond, are unsuitable once details are revealed, or appear to exist only to trigger credit charges.

This platform appears to make money from clicks and dark UX design, not from helping professionals win work. I strongly warn other builders and tradespeople: be extremely careful.

I would not recommend Bark to professionals who value transparency and fair business practices.

I strongly urge Bark to reconsider this policy and introduce a fairer system — or risk losing the trust of genuine service providers.

We deserve transparency, fairness, and value for our investment.

text:
Die Plattform ist von der Software her ganz gut umgesetzt und das Servicepersonal am Telefon und per Email auch sehr nett, daher zwei Sterne (je einen quasi für diese beiden Punkte). 

Bei der Kernfunktion (gute Leads kaufen) konnte ich jedoch leider bisher keine besonders gute Erfahrung machen: Beim ersten Creditpaket war kein einziger Lead dabei, wobei ich jeden Lead sowohl über das System und dann später per manueller Email als auch telefonisch zu erreichen versuchte. Oft klappt das gar nicht erst. Wer bitte schaltet eine Anzeige und lässt sich dann auf keinem der Kommunikationskanäle erreichen, wenn man laut System meist der Einzige war, der den Lead bisher gekauft hat? Das kommt hier aber oft vor. Daher kaufe ich schon gar keine Leads mehr, bei denen die Tel-Nr. nicht verifiziert ist, da diese dann meist nicht vergeben war und per Email (meist web.de, gmx, gmail oder hotmail etc, d.h. keine seriösen eigenen Domains) keine Rückmeldung kam.

Die Leadqualität ist meines Erachtens sehr schlecht und das kann ich auch von daher bewerten, weil ich für meine Firma schon diverse Lead-Kauf-Plattformen ausprobiert habe. Diese Plattform hier zielt bisher scheinbar auf überdurchschnittlich viele Privatpersonen oder Solopreneure bzw. solche, die es werden wollen (z. B. Startups ohne Geld). 

Firmenleads (d.h. im B2B-Bereich) von Interessenten, die ihr Inserat im Auftrag einer Firma schalten, sind erfahrungsgemäß sehr viel ernsthafter und wertiger, können hier aber nicht klar als solche identifiziert werden (wenn überhaupt mal eine Firma hier inseriert). Auch kriegt man vom System nur einen Vornamen, was total unseriös ist in der Ansprache der Leads, weil man sie ohne Namen oder mit Vornamen anschreiben muss.

WUNSCH: Wenn man konkret Leads von Firmen als solche erkennen könnte, wäre das hier ein klarer Vorteil, den ich mir sehr wünsche. Dann würde ich Bark.com nochmal eine Chance geben. Denn nachdem das erste Creditpaket nichts erbrachte, außer viel Zeit- und Geldverschwendung, habe ich eine Erstattung erbeten und erhalten nebst dem Tipp, dass man künftig gleich innerhalb der ersten halben Stunde bei den Inserenten Kontakt suchen sollte. Wenngleich das nicht immer gelingt, war dann (vielleicht durch das bestmögliche Befolgen dieses Tipps) die Konvertierung schon besser: Zwei Kunden beim nächsten Credit-Paket, d.h. zwei von insgesamt zwei Credit-Paketen, mit denen man laut Angabe von Bark.com durchschnittlich 20 Leads kaufen kann. Also beim ersten Paket 0% Konversion, beim zweiten Paket 20%, d.h. durchschnittlich 10% Konversion bei uns bisher.

Leider war die Qualität selbst dieser beiden Leads auch nicht ideal, aber immerhin war eines ein Lead einer Firma (die aber ein extrem niedrigpreisiges Budget hat) und einmal von einem Einzelunternehmer (mit normaler Preisvorstellung). 

Außerdem scheinen viele Leads nicht ernsthaft zu inserieren. I ran a small social services business with the goal of simply covering our costs while helping people in our community. Unfortunately, we could no longer financially sustain it and had to close.

Yelp continued charging me for months afterward, leaving me personally responsible for nearly $1,400 in charges. When I contacted Customer Success, I was initially told I had never canceled and was asked to provide proof. Because the business had already closed and our email accounts had been deleted, I no longer had access to those records.

After pushing them to investigate further, Yelp confirmed that I had canceled my Page Upgrades, but then told me that their records also show my advertising budget nearly tripled on that exact same day. It makes absolutely no sense that a business in the process of shutting down would intentionally cancel & triple the budget in the same day.

My experience with Yelp's advertising and cancellation process has been incredibly shady, the Customer Success team has been misleading and not supportive. After this experience, I cannot recommend Yelp to other small business owners at all.

text:
My Experience With Yelp Advertising – A Warning for Small Business Owners

I am sharing my experience so other small business owners can make informed decisions before signing up for Yelp advertising services.

I was contacted by a Yelp representative and was assisted with setting up an advertising account. During this process, I provided payment information. However, I was never provided a contract by mail, never received a signed agreement, and, to the best of my knowledge, was never emailed any advertising agreement or terms and conditions.

Yelp offered promotional advertising credits as part of the account setup. During the advertising period, I began receiving messages that I believed were not resulting in legitimate business opportunities. In several instances, messages would be received, but after responding, there was no further communication. This raised concerns for me regarding the quality of the leads being generated.

Because of these concerns, I made the decision to cancel my Yelp advertising account. I have documentation showing that the account was canceled, and Yelp’s own records acknowledge the cancellation date.

Despite the cancellation, I was later charged $863. I disputed the charge and attempted to resolve the matter directly with Yelp. Unfortunately, I was unable to obtain a satisfactory resolution through customer service.

I subsequently filed a complaint with my state’s Attorney General’s office. Yelp responded to the Attorney General’s inquiry, but I remained dissatisfied with the company’s position and explanation regarding the charges.

Throughout this process, I repeatedly requested clarification regarding the basis for the charges and any agreement authorizing them. My concern remains that I was charged after cancellation despite my understanding that the account had already been terminated.

I encourage any small business owner considering Yelp advertising to:

• Carefully review all advertising terms and conditions.
• Request copies of any agreements in writing.
• Save all emails, account records, and cancellation confirmations.
• Monitor billing statements closely.
• Document all communications with representatives.
• Keep records of cancellation dates and account activity.

This post reflects my personal experience and opinions based on my records and interactions. Other business owners may have different experiences. I encourage everyone to conduct their own research and maintain thorough documentation when entering into any advertising agreement.

Business Owner,
TTR TAX & NOTARY CO LLC

Yelp has the power to influence public perception, and with that power comes the responsibility to ensure reviews are truthful and balanced. Unfortunately, that has not been my experience.

My experience with Yelp Advertising has been extremely disappointing.

I enrolled in a Yelp advertising program after being offered a promotional credit and was led to believe I would have a clear understanding of the costs and performance of the campaign. Instead, after canceling the program, I was presented with a bill exceeding $1,000 and have spent months attempting to obtain a detailed explanation of how that amount was calculated.

Despite multiple requests, Yelp has failed to provide a complete reconciliation showing:

• The specific services delivered
• How the promotional credits were applied
• Detailed invoices and account ledger information
• Documentation supporting the final balance claimed
• A clear breakdown of advertising performance tied to the charges

What has been most frustrating is the lack of transparency. Yelp continues to state that the balance is correct, yet has not provided the documentation necessary for me to independently verify the charges.

The dispute process has been slow, difficult, and largely unproductive. Escalations resulted in the same generic responses rather than meaningful answers. For a company that serves small businesses, I would expect a much higher level of billing transparency and customer support.

My recommendation to other business owners is simple: read every term carefully, monitor your account frequently, document every conversation, and obtain written confirmation regarding cancellation policies and promotional credits before spending any advertising dollars.

After this experience, I would not advertise with Yelp again and cannot recommend their advertising platform to other small business owners.

Better yet, don't do it.

I am beyond frustrated with Yelp and the way they handle serious issues that directly damage a business’s reputation.

We recently received a negative review from someone who clearly confused our company with another business. This is not the first time — it has happened multiple times. Every time, we report it, explain the situation, and provide context. And every single time, Yelp did absolutely nothing.

This is unacceptable. Incorrect reviews are not harmless — they lower our rating, mislead potential clients, and directly impact our revenue. A platform that profits from businesses should have basic systems in place to verify or remove clearly inaccurate reviews. Yelp chooses not to.

What makes this even worse is the constant pressure to pay for advertising. Yelp has no problem calling, emailing, and pushing for higher monthly payments, yet shows zero urgency when it comes to protecting the businesses that fund their platform.

text:
We gave Yelp every reason to work with us. A complete, polished profile. High-quality photos. Detailed service descriptions. Regular posts. Full case studies documenting our real work for real clients. We responded to every message. We even spent $1,000 on Yelp ads, because we wanted to do things properly.

Then, without warning, Yelp moved two legitimate 5-star reviews into their "Not Recommended" section—effectively hiding them from the public entirely.

These weren't throwaway reviews. They were detailed, genuine testimonials from verified customers. One reviewer posted video footage of the completed job. We built complete case studies around both projects. By any reasonable standard, these were exactly the kind of reviews a consumer platform should want to surface.

But here's where it gets difficult to accept: Yelp's official position is that they didn't remove anything. The reviews are technically still there. They're just hidden from everyone who visits your profile. That distinction—between "hidden" and "deleted"—may protect Yelp legally. In practice, the effect on your business is identical. Your credibility disappears overnight, with no warning and no explanation.

When we reached out to support, we were told it was "the algorithm." No escalation path. No appeals team. No resolution. Just a shrug wrapped in policy language.

Think about what that actually means for small business owners. You can invest months of effort, deliver outstanding work, earn genuine praise from real customers—and a platform's opaque automated system can silently erase that social proof while you're none the wiser. And when you ask why? There's no one there to answer.

Yelp frames this as consumer protection. But hiding authentic feedback from real customers doesn't protect consumers. It misleads them—while simultaneously punishing the businesses that earned those reviews fairly.

To any small business owner reading this: build your reputation on ground that won't shift beneath you. Your own website, your own testimonials, your own channels—places where your work speaks for itself without a third party deciding whether it deserves to be seen. If a platform profits from your ad spend while quietly undermining your credibility, the most rational response is to stop funding it. Redirect that budget somewhere your effort is actually rewarded.

If you absolutely need a third party resource, I'd go with a Google Business Profile and any number of social media platforms before ever considering Yelp.

J'ai récemment fait appel à "Casa Menuiserie" (13270 Fos-sur-Mer) pour l'installation d'une porte moustiquaire avec cadre en aluminium de chez MARITON, équipée d'une toile "air métal" en fils alu tissés.

La commerciale de "Casa Menuiserie" m'a présenté le fournisseur MARITON comme l'un des meilleurs du marché avec des produits de haute qualité.

J'ai donc signé le devis en date du 18 mars 2024 pour une installation prévue le 19 juin 2024.

Malheureusement, mon expérience a été loin d'être satisfaisante.

La porte a dû être remplacée à trois reprises :

- La première fois, la toile n'était pas correctement tendue.
- La deuxième fois, la toile était déchirée (photo ci-jointe).
- La troisième fois, après la pose définitive et paiement du solde, j'ai constaté que la toile était légèrement gondolée sur la partie basse et l'un des bords du cadre présentait des mailles abîmées (photo ci-jointe).

De plus, lors de la pose du cadre en aluminium, "Casa Menuiserie" a endommagé le cadre de ma porte d'entrée en éclatant un gros morceau de crépi (photo ci-jointe).

La société n'a pas fait appel à un maçon pour réparer les dégâts. Le crépi a été sommairement réparé par le menuisier, qui n'est pas du métier.
J'ai donc dû procéder moi-même aux finitions, notamment la peinture de l'encadrement.

Pour une prestation qui m'a coûté 1585 euros TTC (pose comprise), je m'attendais à une qualité et un service bien supérieurs.
Je suis très déçu et ne recommande pas ces entreprises.

text:
I had an extremely disappointing experience with Yell’s website service, and I regret choosing them.

Before signing the contract, I was told the website setup would take about a week before development started. Instead, the entire process dragged on for over a month and became incredibly stressful. I provided every page and all of the content they needed, but the website they produced looked very basic and unprofessional. It honestly felt like it had been built by someone with very little web design experience.

Rather than working with experienced web designers and developers, I found myself teaching their team how to build my own website. I spent four consecutive days explaining how the website should be designed, and even then it was still incomplete.

The booking form was one of the most important parts of my business. I even gave them a working example of how I wanted it built, but they failed to implement it correctly. I also tested the booking system they created, and it leaves customers stuck halfway through the process without taking them anywhere. In my opinion, this is a serious issue that could easily cost businesses potential customers. It seemed they either lacked the technical knowledge or the professional experience needed to build the functionality correctly.

Even their own website checking tools identified numerous issues that required improvement, yet these problems remained unresolved.

During the sales process, I was left with the impression that I was hiring a professional British company that would take care of everything for me. Unfortunately, the reality was very different. Once the contract was signed, I had to chase them constantly for updates and corrections. I called them three times within the first month asking to cancel the contract because I had already lost confidence in their ability to deliver, but my requests were refused.

At the moment, my app shows 21 leads. However, 15 of those were simply test submissions made by Yell themselves while testing my website. Of the remaining six, none resulted in a confirmed booking, and two weren’t even related to my services. From my perspective, this has been a complete loss of time and money.

Another major issue is the tracking phone number they provide. I cannot directly call customers back using that number, so I’m forced to contact them from my personal mobile instead. Many customers don’t answer unknown mobile numbers, which I believe has caused me to lose potential jobs and genuine leads.

I paid around £800 for a website that I don’t believe will help my business. I even accepted that financial loss and asked them to cancel my contract, but because it is a business-to-business agreement, I was told I would still have to continue paying regardless of whether the leads generated turned into actual work.

In my opinion, Yell needs to invest in experienced web developers, professional web designers, and better software if they want to compete in today’s market and deliver the quality of service customers are promised.

This entire experience has caused me an enormous amount of stress and has had a serious impact on my mental wellbeing. What was promised during the sales process was not what I experienced as a customer.

Based on my personal experience, I cannot recommend Yell’s website design service. I strongly advise anyone considering their website package to fully understand what they are agreeing to before signing a contract.

text:
Anyone considering Yell’s services should insist on receiving a complete, itemised description of everything included in the proposed package before signing up. I found the package descriptions vague, which made it difficult to understand precisely what was being purchased and what limitations applied.

I would also strongly recommend obtaining written confirmation of anything explained verbally during the sales process. In my case, I specifically asked whether the website included in the package would use a simple template or could be designed more bespoke to our requirements. I was told that either approach was possible, provided the website did not exceed five pages. After signing the agreement, however, one of the first things I was told was that a bespoke design was not possible.

Experiences like this suggest there are inconsistencies between what is communicated during the sales process and what the delivery teams are actually able or authorised to provide. This needs to be addressed. To be fair, the teams have responded quickly and generally appear responsive, but good communication after purchase does not resolve a lack of clarity before the contract is agreed.

For B2B companies in particular, I would carefully question whether Yell represents the right investment. Yell now appears to operate partly as a digital marketing agency, but its original proposition as a searchable business directory is increasingly difficult to justify. In Google search results, a Yell listing is effectively a directory entry appearing within another search directory. With businesses and consumers increasingly using AI platforms to identify and recommend suppliers, I also saw no clear evidence that Yell has meaningfully integrated AI-driven vendor discovery into its offering.

Based on my experience so far, I cannot currently recommend the service. The packages need to be more clearly itemised, verbal commitments must match what is ultimately delivered, and the overall proposition needs to demonstrate greater relevance in an increasingly AI-led search environment.

I submitted a full listing, was told approval takes 2 days, and heard nothing for 4. I contacted customer service to chase the approval and, at the same time, clearly stated I did not want my phone number published. Nobody told me this was a problem. They said the request had been escalated to get the listing approved.

A day later I got a call that turned out to be a long, mandatory SEO sales pitch, I was asked about pricing, margins, travel radius, website traffic, and more, all framed as necessary to "list my business," while being used to push their paid services. I told the agent repeatedly, multiple times, that I did not want my number listed. He said "OK" each time. At the end of the call, he told me the listing was published. I checked the listing and found my number published, against explicit instructions I'd now given to two separate people. I went to live chat to get it removed. Instead of addressing what I'd actually said, I was met with a wall of scripted "guidelines" language, repeated regardless of what I typed. When I explicitly stated I was revoking my consent under GDPR, they didn't engage with that at all, just more guidelines, as if their internal policy overrides UK data protection law.

This isn't a case of me not understanding how the platform works. I gave clear, repeated, explicit instructions to two different people before anything was published, and was actively reassured both times. Yell published my personal data anyway, then treated a formal GDPR consent withdrawal as something to be managed with a script rather than a legal right. Followed all this up with an unsolicited email telling me what's "wrong" with my SEO.

I've now spent hours dealing with a problem they created, on top of a sales process that used data-gathering as leverage before I'd even agreed to anything.

If you're a business with any reason to keep your number off a public listing, be aware that "no" does not seem to register with their staff until it's already too late.

An enthusiastic sales person lied through his teeth.

My business had a website, SEO, social media, google business listings, bing business listings, PPC. 

I made a listing for my business on Yell and ticked a box that advertised how YELL offered advisory calls as to improvements to business marketing.

Next thing I know I'm getting a pushy caller talking to me like I'm a moron about 'did I have a website?', and 'we (yell) can make you top of the listings on google' - a promise that had yet to be fulfilled. We discussed their offer and I said I'd take a follow up call later in the week.

I did a little back-ground reading and saw various negative reviews on this platform and others, so when I got the follow up call I said I wasn't interested as I had read that you don't get to keep the website afterwards.
I was assured that this wasn't the case and was told (I quote) "No, the website is your is to keep".
So I signed up, and next thing I know I'm being told to hand over the links to my social media and google business accounts and I have to junk my existing website so they (yell) can make a new one for me- I was led to believe that Yell would just lean in and advise me on improvements I could make to my website.

They made the website in WIX which is a basic low performing problematic web builder that offer poor functionality and now my website doesn't transpose effectively between different screen sizes.

The content was terrible AI driven slop that I have had to change myself- I significantly leveraged an uplift in SEO myself, yet am paying yell for the same thing only to get nothing.

I have yet to see my business appear in the google listing at any significant level- to which Yell just say 'well there's a lot of competition' which somewhat undermines the promise made by their sales person that 'we will make you appear in the top listings'

The quoted price turned out to be less VAT so is in fact a significant percentage of my business's monthly turnover- I'm paying 50% of my monthly income to Yell for largely nothing.

Yell decided to create a landline for us that they (yell) own and stuck it all over our listings, so should we leave Yell we lose that phone number.

Having overhauled the website myself, I have found out in the last few weeks that Yell still contractually maintain ownership of it and so should we leave we lose the website and its content.

Google offer direct PPC marketing via google business listings that actually work out cheaper than Yell as Yell charge and admin fee for doing what any business owner can do themselves.

Basically, if all the above means nothing and has confused you, then Yell might work for you- but cheaper options exist. 

If you are a basically competent person with access to AI and know how to find your way around Google, and social media, then stay away as Yell will charge you for doing the most basic of things.

⭐☆☆☆☆ 1 Star

As the owner of OSLID LTD, this has become the worst professional decision I have ever made.

I pay £298 per month to Yell, and, after six months, I have not received a single reliable lead, genuine commercial contract or domestic customer that justifies this investment.

I signed up because I was told my website would be placed on the first page of Google and that, provided I had the capacity, I could expect between one and five potential contracts per month.

I knew £298 per month was a huge financial commitment for me, but I was given confidence that the service would quickly generate enough business to pay for itself.

Six months later, none of that has happened.

Today, if I search for "Commercial Cleaner in London", my website is still nowhere to be found after numerous pages of Google results.

I was also required to replace my own website with a Yell-built website and replace my own business telephone number with Yell's advanced call-tracking number, despite repeatedly explaining that I wanted to keep my original number visible.

The website itself lacked important keywords, and, when I raised this concern, I was effectively told that I could add them myself.

Another major concern was that my website went offline for a week, and I was the person who had to alert Yell about it. I then requested an explanation regarding their website monitoring systems and why nobody informed me that my website was down. I never received a satisfactory answer.

The quality of the contacts generated has also been extremely disappointing. The overwhelming majority were consultants and sales companies trying to sell me additional services rather than genuine customers. Some initially presented themselves in a way that made them appear connected to tender opportunities until I challenged them and discovered they were consultants.

The most disappointing aspect, however, has been how my concerns were handled.

After complaining about the lack of results, instead of resolving my concerns, I felt persuaded into signing another agreement by a sales manager called Sam, despite already being unhappy with the existing service. Within hours, I communicated that I no longer wanted to proceed, but my request was not actioned.

I have also been transparent about my financial hardship. I earn less than £2,000 per month, pay high rent, support my children and cover all my essential living expenses. This situation has now reached the point where I am borrowing money from family and friends to maintain payments for a service that has produced no measurable return.

The anxiety this is causing is enormous because I genuinely do not want to close OSLID LTD.

My advice to Yell is simple: be realistic during the sales process, focus on generating genuine customers instead of sales calls from consultants, proactively monitor the websites you manage, and show flexibility when a struggling small business explains that the service is not working.

At the very least, after six months of poor results, a significant reduction in the monthly fee should have been considered if the objective was to retain me as a customer.

I am not asking for special treatment. I am asking for fairness, transparency and common sense.

My experience with Yell has been extremely disappointing and, unfortunately, what began in January 2026 remains an ongoing saga.

Immediately following a formal review of my campaign, I raised serious concerns regarding lead quality, lead classification, campaign performance and the overall value being delivered. I was informed that my Account Manager carried out an audit with his manager, both agreed there were concerns, and the matter was escalated internally. Despite this, the issues were ultimately rejected and I have yet to receive what I consider to be satisfactory evidence addressing the points raised.

A major concern was the classification of leads. I challenged whether supplier calls, missed calls, existing customers and other non-sales contacts should have been counted towards campaign performance and lead guarantee figures. Despite repeatedly requesting evidence, I do not believe these concerns have been properly addressed.

The performance of the campaign was also deeply concerning. Based on the figures provided to me by Yell, my analysis showed that the effective cost per conversion was in excess of £1,500. For any small business, that level of performance raises serious questions about campaign management, optimisation and value for money.

What makes this particularly frustrating is that since leaving Yell, my business has achieved dramatically different results. Under independent Google Ads management, I have generated more genuine enquiries and secured more new customers in approximately three months than I achieved during the eighteen months Yell managed the account. My current campaign is producing conversions at approximately £48 each and the business is now thriving.

I was also disappointed by the lack of transparency surrounding fees and advertising spend. Google publishes policies for third-party partners that emphasise transparency regarding services, fees and the management of advertising accounts. As a business owner investing significant sums each month, I believe clients should have clear visibility of where their money is being spent and exactly what value is being delivered.

Rather than reaching a satisfactory resolution, this dispute has continued since January and remains unresolved. Throughout the process I have repeatedly requested evidence to support the conclusions being presented, but I have found the responses largely consist of assertions rather than the underlying information required to independently verify the position.

Every business will have its own experience, but mine has been one of ongoing dispute, poor transparency, unresolved concerns and disappointing results relative to the investment made.

There is no lead guarantee, it should be called something else as it appeared to focus almost entirely on the quantity of enquiries rather than the quality of those enquiries.

As a business owner, I don't measure success by how many people contact me. I measure success by how many genuine opportunities are created and how many customers are won.

The impression I was left with was that once a contact had been recorded, the emphasis was on counting it towards the lead target rather than examining whether it represented a realistic sales opportunity for my business.

From my perspective, there seemed to be a significant difference between what Yell considered a lead and what I considered a genuine prospective customer.

That distinction matters because businesses do not grow from lead numbers on a report. They grow from relevant enquiries, quotations, sales and profitable work.

If a supplier call, a missed call, an existing customer, your Auntie or someone looking for a product you do not offer can all contribute towards a lead target, then business owners should look very carefully at how success is being measured before placing too much reliance on a lead guarantee.


If you are considering Yell, I would strongly recommend asking detailed questions about lead validation, campaign management, reporting transparency and exactly how your advertising budget is being allocated before signing any agreement.
Also go over their terms and conditions with a fine tooth comb before signing. 

I see all these 5 star reviews with new customers, lets see how many stars they give in 3 months time.

text:
I signed up with Yell after being given the impression during the sales process that the service would generate a steady flow of genuine enquiries and provide a worthwhile return on investment. The sales presentation was persuasive and created high expectations about the potential results.

Unfortunately, my experience after signing up was very different. Despite paying substantial monthly fees, the volume of genuine leads generated was extremely low and nowhere near what I had been led to expect. The few enquiries received did not come close to justifying the ongoing cost of the service.

What I found particularly frustrating was that when concerns were raised about the lack of results, the suggested solution often appeared to be increasing the advertising spend or upgrading to additional services in the hope of improving performance. In my case, I saw no evidence that spending more money would have delivered a better outcome.

I would also strongly encourage prospective customers to read the contract terms carefully before signing. My impression from the sales discussions was very different from the limitations and disclaimers contained within the agreement. While the sales pitch focused heavily on the results that could be achieved, the contractual terms made it clear that no particular level of enquiries or business could be guaranteed.

Another point prospective customers should be aware of is that business-to-business contracts do not generally provide the same cooling-off rights that consumers may be familiar with. Once committed, I found myself tied into an expensive agreement despite being disappointed with the results delivered.

Advertising always carries risk and no company can guarantee success. However, I felt there was a significant gap between the expectations created during the sales process and the reality of the service delivered. Based on my experience, the return on investment was poor and alternative marketing channels provided considerably better value.

My advice to other small business owners would be to read the contract carefully, understand the cancellation terms before signing, and make sure any expectations discussed during the sales process are reflected in writing. 

Prospective customers should also pay close attention to the website terms. I was surprised to discover that the website provided as part of the package was tied to the ongoing contract and would cease to be available if the agreement ended. Small businesses should make sure they fully understand what they will and will not retain at the end of the contract before signing.

UPDATE (24th June 2026)

As part of the package, Yell provided and managed my website, supplied a dedicated landline number which diverted calls to my mobile, and provided website contact forms through the website they controlled.

This led me to consider how enquiries are attributed and reported. For example, if an existing client refers someone to your business, that person then visits your website to check you out and subsequently contacts you using the published telephone number or contact form, how is that enquiry classified and reported?

I believe prospective customers should understand how website ownership, tracking telephone numbers and website contact forms interact with performance reporting, and should ask detailed questions about the methodology used.

With the benefit of hindsight, I would encourage prospective customers to ask detailed questions about website ownership, call-tracking numbers, lead attribution methodology, and whether the product is a good fit for their industry.

text:
Not for small growing businesses. This will be an in-depth explanation of what I learned from one year with Yell and how yell will keep you trapped at a high price for their services,  leading to small business growth stunting.

TLDR- You won't own your website. The SEO is not good. Barely any leads from yell. Gaslighting and misleading sales pitches. A phone number extension that makes your backlinks unless once you leave yell.

I have a basic background in website design and SEO but went back to a service business. On the first phone call my website was ripped apart and told no one would find it then I was shown a graph of how many more people visit yell that other lead providers so that's how I would get leads (only later when in the contract they tell you they can't guarantee leads). I needed leads and it was made out that my website would be better. 
Down the line I had to redesign my website and fix SEO as it didn't hit any of the services I specifically asked to focus on. I've had to do extra work to fix the SEO so I can get viewed when people search for the terms my business relates to. 
-I called to complain several times about the lack of leads through yell. Yell have an extra "£300p/m" worth of marketing added to attempt to fix this. Nothing changed. I have watched closely the leads that come through yell and those other lead providers that I was shown on the graph initially. Even though I was top in many areas and on several services during my time with the extra marketing with yell I was having barely any leads while I watched many regularly come through other lead providers. This would indicate a misleading pitch by yell that did not apply to me and my area of services. 
-Because of the high cost (to a small business) of this service by yell and lack of leads, it forced me to have to market in other ways to make up the money I needed to pay to yell. I worked out in total that I didn't even make back 1/3rd of the total cost I paid to yell over a year, meaning a loss of 2/3rds the total cost. This was the only marketing I had a loss on over the year and I could have been much more ahead if I had used other marketing options rather than yell. Keep in mind I have several services I can market for, others may struggle more if they rely on 1 service.
-On cancelling the contract your website will get cut off, yell doesn't build you a website like other companies, they rent it to you meaning you have to stay with them at a high cost to keep the website. 
-On one phone call it was attempted gaslighting to say that my chosen marketing wouldn't work yet I was receiving regular jobs from that marketing and barely any from yell. 
-They will add a phone number extension for tracking calls. This was later used to again gaslight me to say how many leads yell was getting me, it was actually coming from the work I had previously put into my google, socials and advertising that had nothing to do with yell. I regularly checked where people found me and rarely did anyone answer yell. The extension number also had bad connection making it difficult to converse with customers, also looking highly unprofessional. My mobile number, which I used in other places to track the difference in lead numbers, never had a delay or connection issue. This extension number is what they will list on all the backlinks to the website meaning the backlinks are only useful while you are with yell. As soon as you cancel all that money you spent with them goes down the drain.

My recommendation- Get a website built by a company who specialise in building and doing SEO but ultimately you own the website and pay for ongoing hosting costs and domain name only. Don't allow anyone to add an extension number that you don't personally own so that your site cant be held hostage by a company. Look up professional reviews of yell to see how they operate.

Disappointing experience – ghosted after three long consultations
​I approached Yell to help streamline our website and manage our advertising. I had three separate, lengthy phone calls with a representative named Matthew, during which we thoroughly discussed our requirements and agreed on a strategy to rebuild our site and launch a campaign.
​Matthew was incredibly eager to secure our business that same day. He initially quoted a rolling monthly price that was slightly over our budget. He then asked if we would be willing to commit to a 12-month contract if he could secure a discount. We agreed, stating that if he could bring the cost down to our budget, we would sign up immediately. Matthew said he needed to get authorisation from his supervisor and promised to call us back by the end of the day.
​That was a week ago, and we have heard absolutely nothing from Matthew or anyone else at Yell.
​This is incredibly poor customer service. We wasted hours explaining our business needs and planning a strategy, only to be completely ghosted. I am very disappointed and certainly would not recommend Yell to any business looking for a reliable partner.

text:
I had been a customer of for around 18 months and always paid on time. I then entered into a new agreement for the Accelerate Tier 5 package with SEO bolt-on at a cost of approximately £2,549 per month plus VAT.

The package was sold heavily around Yell’s “Guaranteed Leads” proposition, which is advertised prominently across their website and sales material as “The UK’s only digital marketing agency that guarantees leads” The package breakdown presented to me was approximately:
• £1,600 Google Ads
• £800 Sponsored Listings
• £450 SEO

Based on those representations, my understanding was that the Google Ads(later discovered via GOTU, white label marketing- not proper Google campaign management as sold) allocation represented substantial actual advertising spend into Google campaigns, while the Sponsored Listings element related to advertising on Yell’s own platform.

However, over time I became increasingly concerned about the transparency of the package, the operation of the Lead Guarantee, and the actual allocation of advertising spend.

The biggest issue for me is that the reality of how the package appears to operate is very different from the impression created during the sales process and marketing. The Yell Web site has it big and bold "The UK’s only digital marketing agency that guarantees leads" Then the live chat pops up and big and bold "Guaranteed Leads, Exclusive to Yell"

For example:
• I later discovered that “margin fees” were embedded within the Google Ads allocation itself
• These management/margin fees were never separately itemised or visibly disclosed to me during the sales process
• The actual media spend versus retained management fees was never transparently reported but is understood to be around 50%. So £1600 Google Ad spend is actually £800 Google Ad spend and £800 for Yell Google Ad management.(This fee is important when we get to the performance)
• The Lead Guarantee itself appears subject to extensive conditions and internal reporting controls that are not obvious from the headline marketing claims.
In simple terms, the “Lead Guarantee” appears to mean:
Yell decide how leads are counted
Yell control the reporting
You still have to pay even if the guarantee is missed
Any credit is usually applied later, not automatically refunded
The guarantee is based on their calculations and definitions, not necessarily what a customer would view as a genuine lead
So while it is technically a “guarantee,” it operates more like:
a conditional account credit system controlled by Yell’s own terms and reporting.

I also formally raised concerns during the live agreement regarding lead delivery, reporting discrepancies, and lead quality. Despite this, no credit was ever disclosed or applied to my account at the time. It was only much later, during collections activity, (5 months later) that Yell alleged a credit had internally been calculated.

Another major concern was campaign performance itself. Yell’s own figures later disclosed over 22,000 clicks resulting in only 8 conversions (click to call, click to email or a form fill), with conversion costs exceeding £1,500 each over a 4 month reporting period. By comparison, my independently managed campaigns are currently achieving significantly stronger results at a fraction of the cost at 26 conversions at £48 per conversion during a 1 month reporting period. (These 26 conversions cost less than one conversion from Yell) The same 26 conversions would cost me £39,000 with Yell where as it costs £1248 with my new managed campaign. This leads to the 50% Google Ad management fee of £800. Are Yell qualified? Results would suggest, "Unlikely"

There were also periods at the start of the agreement where parts of the advertising setup reportedly could not connect properly to Facebook/social campaigns, yet full billing continued and no reconciliation or adjustment of advertising allocation was ever provided.

My concern is that the practical operation of this package, the Lead Guarantee, and the transparency around spend allocation were materially different from the impression created by the sales process and marketing.

Consider the following actions:
• Get a a full written breakdown of actual media spend versus management fees
• Ask exactly how leads are classified and counted (missed calls, supplier calls, same number calling you)
• Ask what happens operationally if the Lead Guarantee is missed. Ask for written clarification on the process via email.
• Request direct platform reporting from Google Ads itself to see your spend v margin/management fees
• Read the full terms and conditions very carefully before signing

This package is far more complex and conditional than the headline “Guaranteed Leads” marketing suggests

We recently had our business website built by Yell. The site went live as planned, but the design feels quite generic and not particularly tailored to our business.

One important point that was not clearly explained during the sales process is the level of access to the Wix platform. The website was presented as being built on Wix, which led us to expect that we would be able to manage the site normally through the Wix editor.

As Wix is generally understood to be a platform that allows clients to manage their own content and SEO, we expected to have full editing access to the platform once the site was live. However, after the site went live we discovered that the access provided is limited contributor access, which restricts some functionality within Wix.

This limitation was not clearly communicated during the sales stage, and after reviewing the agreement we cannot see where this restriction is clearly outlined.

We are currently speaking with Yell to clarify what level of access customers are expected to have. Clearer communication about this during the sales process would help businesses understand what they are signing up for and avoid confusion later.

text:
Avoid this company at all costs.
My experience with Yell has been financially damaging, emotionally draining, and riddled with systemic failures across almost every department I dealt with.

Apologies to Conor the account manager for having to write this.  He was a very nice and helpful guy.  The failings are systematic and nothing to do with him. 

I signed up for what was sold to me as a performance-based acquisition system designed to bring in paying customers. That was repeated across multiple calls and never corrected. In reality, what I received was a stream of low-quality, irrelevant enquiries that did not match the service I provide. This was completely different from the product that was advertised and sold to me.

Over six months, I paid approximately £6,000 for a service that failed on every level:

▪ Zero proactive campaign management

Ads were left switched off for long periods without anyone noticing.
When I asked why basic marketing fundamentals were missing (retargeting, exclusions, lookalikes, job-title targeting), I was told ads are “not proactively managed unless clients complain.” That alone speaks volumes.

▪ Wrong targeting and wrong messaging

Despite providing detailed instructions again and again, Yell repeatedly advertised the wrong message, the wrong offer, and targeted the wrong regions and demographics.

▪ Severe billing issues

Yell took duplicate payments, charged more months than agreed, and then told me to sort it out through my bank - something no reputable company should ever tell a customer. Months later, key refunds still were not resolved.

▪ Complete breakdown in communication

I raised multiple formal complaints.
Not one was acknowledged or responded to within the timeframes they themselves set.
Even now, they have not provided the required resolutions.

▪ Massive impact on my business

Before using Yell, my coaching business was stable with strong client numbers.
After months of failed delivery, wasted ad spend, mismanagement, and time spent correcting their errors, my business fell into serious financial distress.

I was forced to run my own ads at £5/day just to stay visible, because I had no budget left - all my capital was tied up in a system that did not function.

▪ Hours of my own time wasted

I spent countless hours writing emails, rewriting ad copy, guiding their staff, reviewing errors, submitting complaints, and trying to help them deliver the product I had already paid for. None of this work should ever fall on the client.

The only positive

Conor, the account manager, was polite and made genuine efforts - but even he was blocked by Yell’s broken internal systems. The problem is not staff like him. The problem is the structure, the lack of capability, and the systemic failures in the organisation.

Bottom line:

Yell sold me one thing, delivered something completely different, mishandled my payments, ignored my complaints, damaged my business, and wasted months of my time.

I cannot recommend strongly enough that businesses avoid Yell.

There are far better marketing services out there, and many far cheaper ones that will still outperform what I received.

As Yell have not responded or acknowledged my official complaint emails I have had to raise with the ASA, Trading Standards, ICO, CMA and prepare for small claims court.  I appreciate the polite response Penny however I’ve tried to settle this amicably for months now.

I was promised a full digital marketing package from Yell — better visibility on Google, an SEO-optimised website, local and national advertising campaigns, a tool to grow my Google presence, and a dedicated account manager who would guide and manage everything. None of this materialised.

My account manager missed multiple meetings, and when someone finally did attend, they presented a Wix website that was far worse than my existing WordPress site. There were delays, miscommunication, and no advertising campaigns delivered that I am aware of.

The “reputation manager tool” was in my opinion, misleading. It only imports Google reviews into Yell — it does not export Yell reviews to Google, so it offers no help at all in improving Google visibility (despite that being a major part of what I was sold).

Customer service was consistently poor. Meetings were missed without explanation, call-backs never happened, and complaints were passed between departments with no accountability. The only time Yell were reliable was when chasing payment.

Even after admitting the service I received was poor, they still expect me to honour a £500-per-month contract for work that was never delivered. As a small business, this has been expensive, stressful and incredibly disappointing.  I have had to take legal advice as they are calling and emailing constantly threatening debt collection, even though my account is in dispute.

What also concerns me is the pattern of reviews on this page. The majority of 5-star reviews seem to praise individual staff members for being “helpful,” but rarely mention results, performance or actual advertising outcomes. In contrast, the detailed negative reviews describing mis-selling, poor service and a lack of results line up very closely with my own experience. This raise questions for me about how reviews are being gathered or encouraged. This is just my opinion after reading through the reviews.

Based on my experience, I cannot recommend Yell.

text:
My three-month experience with Yell Business has been incredibly disappointing. Despite promising increased traffic through Google ads and their platform, the reality fell short. As the owner of Speed Booking UK, which has flourished via Instagram and Facebook ads, I expected better results. Yell's website design was subpar even after multiple revisions, and the traffic I received was mostly spam calls and texts. Attempting to cancel my £360/month subscription proved futile, as I'm locked into a 12-month contract and faced threats of debt collectors. I urge potential Yell Business customers to explore alternatives like Google, Instagram, or Facebook ads. 

My client manager at Yell has been exceptionally supportive, and everyone I've interacted with has been understanding and helpful given my current circumstances. I have no complaints about any individual on the team. However, my main concern lies with the overall business practices. Entering into a 12-month contract without guaranteeing the expected results for the majority of customers feels unethical.

I'm still seeking to cancel my subscription, but doubt Yell's willingness to prioritize customer satisfaction over profit.

*Updated Review as of 15/09/2025*
Quick update – someone from the Yell team got in touch regarding my issue with the monthly subscription, and they were actually able to switch my package over to Google Ads instead of just promoting on Yell. Once they did that, I started seeing more clicks and better interaction with my business.

To be honest, I think Yell’s business model is focused way too much on pushing you to advertise on their own platform, even though barely anyone actually uses Yell to search for services anymore — most people just Google it. So the fact they prioritise their own listings over running proper Google Ads for you is a bit frustrating.

That said, the person I spoke to was helpful, and after switching to the Google Ads option, I did get better results. I ended up staying on for another 3–4 months before cancelling, which I did straight away once the term ended.

If you’re considering Yell, I’d definitely recommend pushing for the Google Ads package, not just their own platform listings. The listings are technically free, but honestly, the leads you get are low quality and not worth much. Get them to advertise your business on Google — that’s the only way you’ll see real value.

I’ve changed my review from 1 star to 3 stars because they eventually sorted the issue, but I still feel the service overall wasn’t worth the money I was paying.

I submitted a job request through Checkatrade for some tarmac work on my property. I expected to receive responses from interested tradespeople that I could review and decide who I wanted to deal with.

Instead, since Saturday morning I have received approximately 20 phone calls, as well as WhatsApp messages, from different tradespeople regarding the job.

I have now had to submit a formal complaint asking Checkatrade to close the job, stop sharing my contact details and tell me how many businesses my information has been provided to.

Based on my experience, I would not use Checkatrade's quote-request service again. There needs to be much better control over who receives a customer's contact details and a simple, obvious way for customers to stop a job and further contact.

text:
My Experience with Checkatrade Over the Last Six Months

I want to describe my experience with Checkatrade over the last six months and explain what I have personally experienced since joining.

There are several types of customers I have encountered through the platform.

First, we have people who supposedly need a job done remotely, sometimes even thousands of miles away from where you operate. While you are paying for your Checkatrade membership, you constantly have to contact these customers, arrange messages, make calls and spend your valuable time trying to organise the job.

However, sometimes they are actually looking for something else or, in my experience, some enquiries have appeared suspicious or potentially fraudulent. You contact the customer, call them or try to arrange the job, only to discover that the enquiry does not appear to be a genuine job.

When you are paying around £570 per month, you can see how quickly the costs can add up. Over a 12-month membership, that would be approximately £6,840 — nearly £7,000. Imagine spending nearly £7,000 over a year while receiving enquiries that may be unsuitable, unsuccessful or never turn into actual work.

That is a serious concern for a small business.

On the other hand, we have customers who post jobs because they want to compare 20 different companies. They can take up your time in the morning, but they don’t even have the time to send you a message or respond to you. Sometimes, after you have already spent time contacting them, they simply say that they have already found someone.

Then we have another type of customer who is looking for a service but is not actually sure whether they want to proceed. They are simply interested in comparing quotes and seeing how much the service will cost.

Even when they haven’t bought an item, have a house move coming up, or have a specific job they are supposedly looking for, sometimes they are still only looking around and comparing prices.

This is what I have personally experienced during my six months with Checkatrade.

The other issue is Checkatrade’s membership system. They are very busy promoting and selling memberships and encouraging people to pay for the service. However, when you actually experience the lead system, you realise that there is very little control over the quality of the enquiries being sent to you.

From my experience, you can be charged for a lead simply because the enquiry has been sent to you, regardless of whether it becomes a genuine job, whether the customer is serious, or whether the enquiry is suitable for your business.

That is the biggest problem I have experienced.

If I could give advice to another small business considering joining Checkatrade, I would seriously consider using the service on a shorter-term or credit basis rather than committing to a 12-month membership.

In my experience, Checkatrade was not what I understood it to be initially. I don’t feel that the reality of paying for individual leads and dealing with enquiries that may not become genuine jobs was made clear enough at the beginning.

Please do your research before joining. Think carefully before committing to a 12-month membership. Don’t assume every lead is a genuine customer ready to book.

This is my personal experience over the last six months, and I am sharing it so other businesses can make an informed decision before committing their time and money.

For me personally, I would stay away from it.
